case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts may entertain a systemic challenge to DHS border-processing policies and practices that allegedly block or deter asylum seekers from applying for protection at or near ports of entry, or whether Congress has stripped jurisdiction (and limited review to narrow removal-order channels) under the INA.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) jurisdiction- and review-limiting provisions—most centrally 8 U.S.C. § 1252 (including limits on review of immigration enforcement actions and channeling of claims into petitions for review), along with the asylum statute’s application access provisions (e.g., 8 U.S.C. § 1158) and related implementing procedures for inspection/processing at the border.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Government (Secretary Noem/DHS) argues that respondents’ lawsuit is an impermissible attempt to use district-court litigation to supervise or restructure how DHS conducts border inspection, processing, and asylum screening. In the Government’s view, Congress—especially through 8 U.S.C. § 1252—channeled or barred such claims by stripping lower-court jurisdiction over challenges that ‘arise from’ or are ‘in connection with’ immigration enforcement and removal processing, requiring claims to proceed (if at all) only through the INA’s limited, individualized review mechanisms tied to removal proceedings or removal orders. The Government also leans on Supreme Court precedent emphasizing (i) the political branches’ primacy over admission/entry, (ii) the limited constitutional and statutory rights of noncitizens seeking initial entry, and (iii) strict limits on habeas and judicial review in the expedited-removal context—contending these principles foreclose systemic APA/constitutional suits aimed at border-policy operations.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Al Otro Lado and aligned amici contend their challenge is not a backdoor appeal of any particular removal order, but a systemic challenge to DHS policies and practices that unlawfully prevent or obstruct access to the asylum process itself (including the ability to present at ports of entry and lodge an asylum claim). They argue § 1252’s channeling/bar provisions should not be read to eliminate all judicial oversight of widespread, programmatic conduct that effectively nullifies statutory asylum rights and violates the APA and/or the Constitution, particularly where many affected individuals are not yet in removal proceedings and therefore cannot realistically obtain review through the INA’s removal-order pathways. Respondents further maintain that Supreme Court decisions limiting habeas for expedited removal (such as Thuraissigiam) are distinguishable because those cases involve post-entry challenges to an individual’s expedited-removal order, whereas this case concerns access to the asylum application process and agency compliance with governing statutes and procedures.
key_precedents: Department of Homeland Security v. Thuraissigiam, 140 S. Ct. 1959 (2020)
Sale v. Haitian Centers Council, Inc., 509 U.S. 155 (1993)
RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community, 136 S. Ct. 2090 (2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: if individuals are turned away before any proceeding begins, the petition-for-review channel may be practically unavailable, and we should not convert § 1252(b)(9) into a jurisdictional catchall. But the claims as pleaded and, especially, the relief sought would require a district court to supervise frontline inspection and screening decisions that determine whether removal-related processing begins at all—matters Congress placed within its tightly reticulated channeling and limitation scheme in § 1252(b)(9) and, as Justice Alito emphasizes, foreclosed as systemwide injunctive relief by § 1252(f)(1). Whatever residual concern remains about “no meaningful review” in some applications cannot supply jurisdiction Congress withheld, and the appropriate course is a narrow disposition dismissing for lack of jurisdiction (and, in any event, recognizing § 1252(f)(1)’s remedial bar) without foreclosing whatever individualized review Congress did authorize where it is available.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that some individuals are allegedly turned away before any removal proceeding begins, so a petition for review may be practically unavailable. But Congress wrote § 1252 to channel—and in key respects to foreclose—judicial review of claims bound up with the inspection-and-removal apparatus, and that jurisdictional design does not turn on whether an alternative forum exists in every application. As the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize, respondents’ requested systemwide injunction would necessarily supervise frontline screening and decisions inseparable from commencing and administering removal processing, bringing the suit within § 1252(b)(9) and § 1252(g) and running headlong into § 1252(f)(1)’s bar on lower-court orders that “enjoin or restrain the operation” of the relevant provisions. The absence of a congressionally authorized cause of action and review vehicle for programmatic relief is not an invitation for the Judiciary to create one outside the INA’s scheme.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s “no meaningful review” point is the hardest, but it cannot overcome the text and structure Congress enacted in § 1252 to channel and, in key respects, to preclude district-court oversight of the inspection-and-removal machinery. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, the claims and requested relief are not merely about a past wrong to discrete individuals; they would entail forward-looking judicial supervision of frontline screening decisions that determine whether the statutory removal apparatus is set in motion, placing them within the heartland of § 1252’s channeling provisions. Moreover, even if one were to accept Justice Jackson’s effort to recharacterize this as an antecedent “access-to-process” claim, § 1252(f)(1) confirms that Congress withheld lower-court authority to issue the kind of programmatic injunction respondents seek, and the asserted absence of an alternative vehicle cannot supply jurisdiction Congress denied. The proper course is to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction (and, independently, to recognize the remedial bar), while leaving whatever individualized review Congress has authorized in cases that proceed through the statutory pipeline.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that Congress meant to prevent district-court “supervision” of border processing, and that the requested relief would effectively regulate how DHS conducts inspection and expedited-removal screening. But that argument depends on treating these as claims “arising from” removal proceedings when, as pleaded, many individuals are blocked from ever entering any proceeding at all—so the petition-for-review channel is not merely inconvenient but nonexistent for the very injury alleged, a distinction Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson correctly press. Our precedents (as in Jennings) caution against converting § 1252(b)(9) into a catchall for any immigration-related claim, and § 1252(g)’s focus on three discrete prosecutorial actions does not naturally encompass an antecedent, categorical obstruction of the statutory process itself. Even accepting Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on § 1252(f)(1), that provision is remedial and cannot be read to render alleged unlawful executive detention/obstruction functionally unreviewable in a manner that would invite serious Suspension Clause and due process concerns.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Alito press the best point for Petitioner: Congress in 1996 meant to prevent district-court “supervision” of removal processing, and respondents’ requested relief looks programmatic and forward-looking. But under Thunder Basin—and consistent with Jennings—our inquiry is claim-specific, and these pleadings allege a categorical obstruction that prevents proceedings from ever beginning, so the petition-for-review channel is not merely inconvenient but, for many, nonexistent; that is the opposite of “meaningful” review. Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett respond that lack of an alternative forum cannot create jurisdiction Congress withheld, but that assumes § 1252(b)(9) and § 1252(g) actually reach this antecedent access-to-process claim; § 1252(g)’s three discrete actions and (b)(9)’s “arising from” language fit poorly where the injury is being denied entry into the statutory scheme altogether. I agree with Justice Alito that § 1252(f)(1) may sharply constrain the remedy (especially classwide injunctions), but that remedial limit does not answer the antecedent jurisdictional question whether a district court may adjudicate a claim that otherwise risks being effectively unreviewable.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the hardest point: if some individuals are turned away before any proceeding begins, channeling into the petition-for-review pipeline may be practically unavailable and risks leaving no avenue for relief. But Congress wrote § 1252(b)(9) to sweep in “all questions of law and fact … arising from any action taken … to remove an alien,” and these claims—attacking frontline processing decisions that determine whether removal screening occurs at all—are still “arising from” removal action in the ordinary sense and within the INA’s carefully circumscribed review scheme. Jennings cautions against treating (b)(9) as a catchall, but it does not license us to disregard Congress’s chosen channel where the suit would, as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize, entail programmatic judicial supervision of inspection and screening. And even if one harbored doubts about channeling at the margins, § 1252(f)(1) independently bars the forward-looking, systemwide injunction sought here, reinforcing both the statutory design and the redressability limits for this district-court action as pleaded.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest point: some individuals are allegedly turned away before any proceeding begins, so the petition-for-review channel may be nonexistent for them. But as the Chief Justice explains, the claims and the requested forward-looking relief are inseparable from DHS’s frontline inspection/screening and the initiation (or non-initiation) of removal-related processing—precisely the kind of removal-adjacent administration Congress tightly channeled and constrained in § 1252(b)(9) and § 1252(g), rather than leaving to systemwide district-court supervision. The absence of a “meaningful” alternative forum in some applications cannot itself create jurisdiction Congress withheld, particularly where the suit seeks programmatic control over enforcement and processing choices for which courts lack manageable standards. And, as Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 1252(f)(1) independently forecloses the broad injunctive relief sought here, which reinforces the conclusion that this district-court suit—as pleaded—cannot proceed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: if individuals are turned away before any proceeding begins, the petition-for-review pathway may be unavailable, and § 1252(b)(9) should not be treated as a catchall. But the threshold inquiry remains what Congress enacted, and § 1252’s text and structure reflect a deliberate choice to channel—and in key respects to preclude—district-court suits that would regulate how DHS conducts inspection and threshold screening that determines whether removal processing begins at all, as the Chief Justice emphasizes. The absence of an alternative review vehicle in some applications does not authorize courts to create jurisdiction Congress withheld, particularly where respondents seek programmatic, forward-looking relief. And even if one were to doubt the breadth of (b)(9) or (g) in a subset of applications, Justice Alito’s § 1252(f)(1) point independently confirms Congress’s decision to bar lower-court injunctions that would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of these provisions, foreclosing the remedy this suit is built around.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s “inseparable” framing forcefully captures Congress’s evident desire to prevent district courts from running removal processing, and Justice Alito is right that § 1252(f)(1) likely forecloses much of the systemwide injunctive relief respondents seek. But those remedial limits do not transform § 1252(g)—which, by its text, targets only three discrete actions—into a roving jurisdictional bar over antecedent conduct that allegedly blocks access to the very inspection/asylum process Congress created, especially in light of Jennings’s caution against catchall readings. Likewise, § 1252(b)(9) channels claims “arising from” removal actions into the PFR pipeline, and Justice Kagan’s point remains decisive here: on these pleadings, many individuals are allegedly turned away before any proceeding exists, so the channel is not merely inconvenient but illusory for this access-to-process claim. I would therefore preserve district-court jurisdiction to adjudicate the statutory-violation question while separately recognizing that § 1252(f)(1) may significantly constrain the available relief.

John Roberts.reasoning: Before reaching the merits, I would begin with reviewability and jurisdiction: respondents’ suit seeks district-court supervision of DHS’s border inspection and asylum-screening operations in a way that is tightly bound up with the Government’s decisions about how and whether to initiate, conduct, and execute inadmissibility and removal processing. Section 1252’s channeling provisions—particularly § 1252(b)(9) (consolidating review of questions “arising from” removal proceedings) and § 1252(g) (limiting review of claims “arising from” the decision to commence proceedings, adjudicate cases, or execute removal orders)—are best read, in statutory structure and in light of our precedents, to preclude this kind of systemic collateral challenge outside the INA’s specified review mechanisms. Because many of the alleged practices are inseparable from the processing that determines whether an applicant is placed into expedited removal or other proceedings, the requested relief would effectively reallocate responsibilities Congress assigned to the political branches at the threshold of admission, and it would circumvent the limited, individualized channels Congress provided for judicial review. On that threshold ground, I would conclude the district court lacks jurisdiction to entertain the suit as pleaded, without opining on whether particular individual claims might be reviewable in the statutorily prescribed manner.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Congress established a comprehensive and exclusive review scheme in § 1252, making a petition for review the “sole and exclusive means” to obtain judicial review of matters Congress tied to removal/inspection and barring other routes that “arise from” or are “in connection with” those processes. Respondents’ requested systemic injunctions and APA/constitutional claims would necessarily supervise and restructure DHS’s border inspection and asylum-screening operations at ports of entry—conduct that is part and parcel of the inspection-and-removal machinery Congress insulated from broad district-court oversight through § 1252(a)(5), (b)(9), and (g), and for which Congress did not create a freestanding cause of action outside the INA’s channels. Even if respondents characterize the suit as “programmatic” and not aimed at any particular final removal order, the text and structure of § 1252 foreclose using district-court litigation as an alternative review vehicle when the claims are inseparable from how DHS initiates and carries out enforcement and processing decisions at the border. Consistent with separation-of-powers restraint and this Court’s refusal to expand review mechanisms beyond those Congress enacted, the proper disposition is dismissal for lack of jurisdiction (or limitation to whatever narrow review Congress expressly authorized).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Congress in IIRIRA constructed a highly reticulated scheme for screening and adjudicating protection claims at the threshold, and it paired that design with broad channeling and jurisdiction-limiting provisions in 8 U.S.C. § 1252 to prevent district courts from supervising the Executive’s day-to-day border processing. On these facts, respondents’ “systemic” APA/constitutional suit is, in substance, a challenge to how DHS implements inspection and expedited-removal-related determinations at and near ports of entry—matters that § 1252(b)(9) and § 1252(g) are designed to funnel into (and limit to) the statute’s specified review pathways tied to removal proceedings or removal orders. Whatever the merits of respondents’ allegations about obstruction or deterrence, the INA’s text and structure show Congress chose speed, screening stages, and restricted judicial review as central features of the 1996 scheme, and courts are not free to create an additional programmatic review mechanism in district court. At a minimum, the requested forward-looking, systemwide relief would run headlong into § 1252(f)(1)’s unmistakable limitation on lower-court authority to “enjoin or restrain” the operation of Part IV, confirming that Congress withheld the kind of remedy respondents seek.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Properly framed, respondents do not seek an order admitting anyone or overturning any particular removal decision; they challenge systemic DHS practices at and near ports of entry that allegedly prevent “arriving” noncitizens from even accessing the asylum and inspection procedures Congress mandated in §§ 1158(a)(1) and 1225. Reading § 1252 to bar all district-court review here would render the Executive’s alleged nullification of those statutory procedures functionally unreviewable for many affected individuals who are never placed into removal proceedings and thus cannot reach the petition-for-review channel—an outcome difficult to square with the constitutional backstops that forbid insulating unlawful executive detention or exclusion practices from meaningful judicial scrutiny. Thuraissigiam does not compel that result because it concerned a post-entry, individualized habeas attempt to obtain “additional” asylum process after an expedited-removal order, whereas this suit targets antecedent, programmatic obstruction of access to the congressionally created application process itself. Consistent with over a century of habeas and due-process tradition rejecting rigid historical matching and resisting “downplaying” of claims, § 1252 should not be construed to foreclose review of unlawful systemic barriers to invoking the protection Congress made available to “any alien … who arrives … whether or not at a designated port of arrival.”

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Congress can and often does channel immigration-related review, but the question under my approach is claim-specific: whether these respondents’ particular systemic “asylum-access” claims are of the type Congress intended to be reviewed only within the INA’s removal-order structure. Applying the Thunder Basin framework, routing this challenge exclusively into petitions for review of individual removal orders would not provide meaningful judicial review for many affected would-be applicants who, as alleged, are turned away or deterred at or near ports of entry and therefore never reach removal proceedings (or any final order) that could generate a petition for review. And while DHS has expertise in inspection and processing, the gravamen here is not case-by-case discretionary enforcement but an alleged categorical practice that prevents initiation of the statutory asylum process—an issue that does not fit the INA’s customary, order-centric review path under § 1252(a)(5) and § 1252(b)(9) as construed not to sweep in all claims merely “related to” immigration. Because the INA’s comprehensive scheme does not, on these facts, supply an adequate alternative channel for these access-to-process claims, I would allow district-court jurisdiction to entertain them.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA’s text reflects Congress’s decision to “carefully circumscribe” judicial review of claims bound up with the inspection, screening, and removal machinery, and § 1252(b)(9) channels claims “arising from” actions taken to remove an alien into the petition-for-review process rather than broad district-court supervision of DHS border operations. Respondents’ suit, though styled as “systemic,” seeks exactly that sort of restructuring relief—an order compelling or reconfiguring how officers process would-be applicants at or near ports of entry—and thus collides with Congress’s forum-and-timing instructions in § 1252 and the limited, individualized review paths it supplies. Even assuming some plaintiffs lack an immediate removal-order vehicle, that policy concern cannot overcome the statute’s channeling and jurisdiction-limiting terms, and in any event the requested injunctive relief runs headlong into § 1252(f)(1)’s command that lower courts generally may not “enjoin or restrain the operation of” the relevant INA provisions. Given these threshold constraints on jurisdiction and remedy, Article III redressability is also doubtful because a district court cannot provide the systemic injunction respondents seek within the remedial limits Congress imposed.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The threshold question is reviewability and jurisdiction, not the underlying legality of DHS’s border-processing practices. Respondents’ systemic APA/constitutional suit effectively asks a district court to supervise and restructure how the Executive conducts inspection, processing, and asylum screening at the border—an area where Congress in IIRIRA deliberately channeled and restricted judicial review through 8 U.S.C. § 1252, and where courts generally lack manageable standards to second-guess operational prioritization and processing decisions that implicate foreign affairs and border security. Section 1252’s channeling/stripping provisions—read in light of IIRIRA’s structural purpose to protect Executive discretion—foreclose broad programmatic challenges that “arise from” or are “in connection with” the commencement/administration of removal and related processing, absent a clear congressional statement authorizing this kind of systemic suit and remedy. Whatever the merits of respondents’ statutory allegations, the proper accountability mechanisms are the political branches and the INA’s specified, limited review pathways, not a free-standing district-court injunction restructuring DHS border operations.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The threshold question is jurisdiction, and the text and structure of § 1252 indicate Congress channeled review of claims “arising from” or “in connection with” immigration inspection, expedited-removal screening, and removal processing into the INA’s specified mechanisms (principally the petition-for-review/removal-order scheme), rather than freestanding district-court supervision of border operations. Respondents’ suit—though styled as “systemic”—targets DHS’s policies and practices at ports of entry that govern who may initiate asylum screening and how those determinations are made, which are integral to the admission/exclusion and removal-processing system Congress placed largely in the political branches’ control. Reading § 1252 in context (including its channeling provisions and limits on equitable relief), Congress used sufficiently specific language and a coherent scheme to foreclose district-court jurisdiction for broad programmatic challenges that would effectively restructure frontline border processing. Where the statute is clear, the presumption of reviewability does not supply jurisdiction the INA withholds, and the judiciary’s role remains limited outside the narrow legal/constitutional questions Congress expressly preserves through the statutory review pathways.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Parsing § 1252’s text and structure, the Government’s broad channeling theory stretches § 1252(b)(9) beyond what Congress wrote: respondents’ claim targets allegedly unlawful, systemic front-end border-processing practices that block access to the asylum-application mechanism itself, rather than seeking review of “a final order of removal” (§ 1252(a)(5)) or raising an issue that can be meaningfully funneled through an individual removal case. Under Jennings, § 1252(b)(9) is not a “catchall” bar for any claim that is factually related to immigration enforcement; it channels only those claims that truly “arise from” removal proceedings, and many affected individuals here are never placed into proceedings (or are deterred from presenting), making the removal-order pathway illusory for this systemic access-to-process challenge. Nor does Thuraissigiam control, because it addressed habeas review of an individual expedited-removal order under § 1252(e)’s narrow limits, whereas this suit contests alleged obstruction of the statutory opportunity to apply for asylum at or near ports of entry under § 1158 and related inspection/referral duties. Respecting Congress’s review limits while preserving review of legal questions, I would permit district-court jurisdiction at least to adjudicate whether DHS policies categorically contravene the governing statutes and regulations, without converting that inquiry into review of discretionary or factbound asylum determinations.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts may hear a suit challenging DHS’s policies and practices at the U.S.–Mexico border that allegedly prevent or delay noncitizens from seeking asylum, or whether immigration-channeling/jurisdiction-stripping provisions require dismissal because the claims must be brought only through the INA’s limited review scheme tied to removal proceedings.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Primarily the Immigration and Nationality Act’s judicial-review channeling and jurisdiction-limiting provisions (including 8 U.S.C. § 1252 and related subsections governing review of removal-related claims), alongside statutory asylum access provisions (e.g., 8 U.S.C. § 1158’s right to apply for asylum) and, to the extent constitutional claims are raised, the Suspension Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 2) and Due Process Clause (Fifth Amendment).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (DHS and officials) argue that respondents’ claims—though framed as challenges to border “access” practices—are functionally challenges to the removal/expedited-removal system and thus fall within the INA’s exclusive, carefully channeled review regime; under § 1252’s broad limits on district-court jurisdiction (and related provisions), the suit must be dismissed because Congress required such disputes to be litigated, if at all, through the statutory review process connected to removal proceedings, and Supreme Court precedent (including DHS v. Thuraissigiam and extraterritoriality principles associated with Sale) supports restricting judicial review and remedies for noncitizens at or outside the border.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Al Otro Lado and associated plaintiffs) contend their case targets unlawful, systemic barriers that prevent people from even initiating the asylum process (e.g., being turned back, blocked from presenting at ports, or denied the chance to seek protection), not a final removal order or the validity of removal proceedings; therefore § 1252’s channeling/jurisdiction-stripping provisions do not apply (or do not reach these pre-removal, access-to-process claims), and the courts retain authority to enforce statutory asylum procedures and constitutional minima; they further argue that cases like Sale are inapposite to the specific statutory and procedural rights at issue, and that Thuraissigiam is limited to habeas and expedited-removal review of an individual’s removal order rather than systemic suits to ensure access to the asylum application process.
key_precedents: Sale v. Haitian Centers Council, Inc., 509 U.S. 155 (1993)
RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Cmty., 136 S. Ct. 2090 (2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “access-to-process” framing raises the most serious concern: if plaintiffs are turned away before any proceeding begins, channeling under § 1252(b)(9) could risk practical unreviewability. But as Justice Kagan explains, the question is forum, and the text and structure of § 1252 reflect Congress’s comprehensive channeling of claims that, in substance, seek to regulate the inspection-and-screening machinery under § 1225; the relief requested here would do exactly that, inviting the district court to supervise front-line intake practices in the teeth of IIRIRA’s consolidation design. The stark consequence of accepting respondents’ reading—systemic APA litigation in district court over threshold processing decisions—confirms the better reading of (b)(9), especially in light of Thuraissigiam’s recognition that Congress may sharply limit review at the threshold of entry. To accommodate remaining concerns, our holding should be narrow: resolve jurisdiction (and, if necessary, note § 1252(f)(1)’s independent remedial bar) while reserving what individualized avenues, if any, remain in particular cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “access-to-process” framing is the hardest point: if the alleged wrong occurs before proceedings begin, channeling could, as a practical matter, make review difficult. But § 1252(b)(9) does not turn on formal labels; it sweeps in claims “arising from” the inspection and screening machinery Congress made the gateway to removal and asylum processing, and respondents’ requested relief would directly regulate DHS’s administration of § 1225 at the front end. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, the question is forum, and Congress made the final order the linchpin while providing specified, limited review paths (including the systemic vehicle in § 1252(e)(3)); we may not create a freestanding district-court alternative by invoking constitutional-avoidance. Any residual concern about remedy is further addressed, as Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch note, by § 1252(f)(1)’s separate bar on classwide injunctions that would “enjoin or restrain” the statute’s operation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “access-to-process” framing is the strongest counter: if proceedings never meaningfully begin, channeling into removal-linked review could seem ill-suited and potentially leave some claims hard to litigate. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, § 1252(b)(9)’s text and Congress’s evident design sweep broadly over claims that, in substance, arise from the § 1225 inspection and screening machinery, and respondents’ requested relief would amount to district-court supervision of that front-end system—the very end-run IIRIRA sought to prevent. Whatever edge cases might exist, Congress supplied specific, limited review paths (including the systemic avenue in § 1252(e)(3)), and we should not create a freestanding APA forum simply because plaintiffs prefer programmatic relief. In any event, as Justice Gorsuch notes, § 1252(f)(1) independently forecloses the classwide injunction here because it would "enjoin or restrain" the operation of the relevant INA provisions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take seriously the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s contention that § 1252(b)(9) should be read broadly to consolidate challenges tightly connected to § 1225 inspection and screening, and that Thuraissigiam permits sharp limits on threshold review. But that argument depends on recharacterizing the pleadings: these respondents allege they were prevented from accessing the very statutory processes Congress created (inspection, referral, credible-fear screening), so their claims do not “arise from” removal proceedings in any ordinary sense when proceedings never meaningfully begin. Channeling “access-to-process” challenges into a removal-linked scheme risks practical—and thus constitutional—unreviewability, implicating the Suspension Clause’s historical backstop and due process concerns that counsel against an expansive reading of jurisdiction-stripping absent a clear statement. As Justice Jackson notes, § 1252(f)(1) may constrain classwide injunctions, but remedial limits cannot substitute for jurisdiction to adjudicate core legality/procedural challenges in the first place.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “access-to-process” framing is the hardest point: if the asserted injury is being turned away before any removal proceeding begins, channeling into removal-linked review can look like no review at all. But as I read § 1252(b)(9), the relevant question is forum, and these claims—seeking orders governing who gets inspected, screened, and referred under § 1225 and expedited-removal procedures—are, in substance, challenges to the operation of the inspection/removal machinery and therefore “arise from” it in the channeling sense Chief Justice Roberts describes. Under Thunder Basin/Elgin, meaningful review remains through the INA’s specified avenues, including case-linked review when proceedings occur and the limited systemic vehicle Congress created in § 1252(e)(3); that Congress did not provide a freestanding APA district-court path is part of the design, not a gap we may fill. Justice Jackson’s concern about proceedings that never begin is real, but it cannot overcome the statute’s consolidation function, and in any event § 1252(f)(1) (as Justices Gorsuch and Alito emphasize) confirms Congress’s intent to prevent lower-court programmatic injunctions restructuring this system.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to worry about “access-to-process” claims that may never culminate in a removal proceeding, and our law generally presumes judicial review absent a clear statement. But the clear statement is here: § 1252(b)(9) channels claims “arising from” the inspection and removal machinery, and—as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain—the relief sought would directly supervise DHS’s implementation of § 1225 screening and referral, the very operational heart Congress meant to consolidate and keep out of freestanding district-court APA litigation. Even if one hesitated at the outer bounds of (b)(9), § 1252(f)(1) independently withholds from lower courts the power to issue the classwide, programmatic injunction respondents request because it would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of these provisions. Constitutional-avoidance concerns cannot supply jurisdiction or remedies Congress has expressly withheld, especially given the INA’s carefully reticulated review scheme.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that respondents allege pre-proceeding “access” barriers and that broad channeling could make those claims practically unreviewable. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the INA’s text and structure reflect Congress’s decision to funnel claims that would regulate the § 1225/expedited-removal screening pipeline into the statute’s specified review mechanisms, rather than freestanding APA suits in district court; the relief sought here would, in substance, reorder that pipeline. Any constitutional-avoidance intuition cannot create jurisdiction Congress withheld, particularly after Thuraissigiam’s recognition that Congress may sharply limit review for recent entrants at the threshold. And even assuming some sliver of jurisdiction, Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito are right that § 1252(f)(1) independently forecloses the kind of classwide, programmatic injunctive relief respondents seek.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that these are pre-proceeding “access-to-process” claims and that a broad reading of § 1252(b)(9) risks practical unreviewability. But as Justice Kagan explains, the inquiry is one of forum: respondents’ requested relief would supervise and restructure the § 1225 inspection/screening machinery, and Congress wrote § 1252’s channeling provisions to prevent precisely that kind of district-court, programmatic oversight, instead routing review through specified mechanisms (including § 1252(e)(3) for systemic challenges). Thuraissigiam reinforces that at the threshold of entry Congress may sharply limit both the scope and forum of review, so constitutional-avoidance concerns cannot be used to manufacture jurisdiction the statute withdraws. And even if some claim survived channeling, Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito are right that § 1252(f)(1) independently forecloses the classwide injunctive relief sought here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the structural one: § 1252 reflects a comprehensive channeling scheme, and the relief requested would plainly regulate how DHS runs the § 1225 inspection/screening pipeline. But the controlling text in § 1252(b)(9) still limits consolidation to claims that “arise from” removal proceedings, and—as Justice Sotomayor emphasizes—the pleaded injury here is being denied access to the very statutory process that would initiate or meaningfully constitute such proceedings, making it difficult to treat these claims as arising from proceedings that never begin. Absent a clearer statement, I am not prepared to read (b)(9) to render antecedent access-to-process legality challenges effectively unreviewable, especially where § 1252(g) (as construed in AADC) does not naturally cover them. I agree with Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch, however, that § 1252(f)(1) likely imposes substantial remedial limits even if jurisdiction exists to adjudicate the underlying legal questions.

John Roberts.reasoning: Read in context and as a whole, §1252’s channeling provisions—especially §1252(b)(9) and §1252(g)—reflect Congress’s intent to funnel into the INA’s review scheme claims that, in substance, challenge how the Executive initiates and conducts the process of deciding admissibility and removal. Although respondents style their suit as a systemic “access-to-asylum-process” challenge, the specific practices alleged (turnbacks, delays at ports, and barriers to triggering credible-fear/asylum processing) are tightly bound up with the Government’s decisions about inspection, admission, and the commencement and execution of removal-related processes, and permitting district-court APA suits here would create the stark consequence of end-running the “exclusive” review pathway Congress established. Thuraissigiam confirms that Congress may sharply limit judicial review for noncitizens at the threshold of entry and that attempts to recast such disputes as broader procedural claims cannot expand review beyond what the INA authorizes. Because the claims are effectively removal-process claims and not properly within district-court jurisdiction, the suit must be dismissed (or at minimum confined to the INA’s specified avenues of review).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Congress made the “final order of removal” the linchpin of judicial review and required that challenges “arising from” the removal system proceed, if at all, through the INA’s exclusive petition-for-review mechanism. Although respondents style their suit as a systemic “access to asylum” challenge at ports of entry, the relief sought would necessarily regulate how DHS initiates, processes, and adjudicates protection claims at the threshold—matters that are inextricably bound up with, and arise from, the statutory machinery for determining removability and eligibility for relief. Sections 1252(a)(5) and 1252(b)(9) thus channel these claims away from district court, and any jurisdiction-restoring exception must be read narrowly and cannot be expanded to authorize broad programmatic suits untethered to the INA’s specified review scheme. Because respondents’ claims do not fit within the limited, textually defined avenues Congress preserved, the complaint must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s text establishes a comprehensive, channeled scheme for litigating removal-related disputes, and respondents’ “access to asylum” challenge—aimed at DHS practices at the border that determine whether noncitizens are processed into (or kept out of) the removal/asylum system—“aris[es] from” the inspection, expedited-removal, and removal framework Congress placed under § 1252’s exclusive review rules. Allowing a district-court, systemic suit for broad injunctive/declaratory relief would improperly bypass that scheme, inviting the very end-run around Congress’s channeling choices that § 1252(b)(9) and related provisions are designed to prevent. In any event, the classwide, programmatic relief sought would “restrain or enjoin” the operation of the relevant INA provisions and thus is barred by § 1252(f)(1), which does not permit lower courts to issue across-the-board relief against DHS’s administration of the removal system. Given Congress’s jurisdictional limits and this Court’s insistence that such limits be enforced as written, the suit should be dismissed (or, at minimum, stripped of the requested systemic remedies) rather than adjudicated on the merits in district court.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Properly characterized from the pleadings, respondents do not seek review of any individual removal order or asylum merits determination; they challenge systemic “turnback/queue management” practices that allegedly prevent noncitizens from ever accessing the statutory process to apply for asylum in the first place. Treating those access-to-process claims as “arising from” removal proceedings under § 1252(b)(9) (or as barred by other channeling provisions) would mischaracterize the relief and make the legality and adequacy of frontier procedures functionally unreviewable, contrary to longstanding practice that courts may hear procedural and legality challenges even in the immigration context. Because Congress must speak unmistakably to foreclose such core judicial oversight—and because channeling into removal-review mechanisms is ill-suited where the alleged injury is denial of process before proceedings meaningfully begin—district-court jurisdiction remains available at least to adjudicate statutory and constitutional claims seeking compliance with lawful procedures. Reading § 1252 expansively to bar these claims would also raise serious constitutional concerns by hollowing out the Suspension Clause/due process backstops where no meaningful alternative review exists.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Our task is not to decide whether DHS’s border practices are lawful, but where those challenges may be heard. The INA sets up a “carefully channeled” review scheme in § 1252 that broadly precludes district-court jurisdiction over claims “arising from” the inspection/admission and expedited-removal machinery, and respondents’ requested relief—orders restructuring how officers process would-be asylum seekers at ports and the border—targets that very system even if styled as a pre-removal “access” claim. Under Thunder Basin/Elgin, meaningful judicial review remains available through the statutory pathways Congress provided (including case-linked review in removal proceedings and the limited systemic vehicle in § 1252(e)(3) for expedited-removal policies), and the agency has expertise in administering inspection, credible-fear, and related screening procedures in the first instance. To the extent some plaintiffs are not in proceedings, that posture underscores the channeling problem rather than creating jurisdiction, because Congress chose to tie review to the removal framework and sharply limited freestanding, programmatic suits in district court.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA’s text channels review of claims “arising from” the Government’s inspection, admission, and removal machinery into the statute’s specified review paths, and respondents’ challenge to border “turnbacks” and delays is, in practical and legal effect, a challenge to how DHS administers the § 1225 screening and referral process that determines who may enter and who will be placed in (or kept out of) removal proceedings. Reading § 1252(a)(5) and especially § 1252(b)(9) in context, this suit seeks to litigate in district court questions Congress directed to be raised, if at all, through the INA’s removal-linked review scheme rather than via a freestanding systemic action. And even assuming injury, the redress respondents seek largely sounds in broad injunctive relief directing how DHS must implement the border screening system, relief that runs headlong into § 1252(f)(1)’s limits on lower-court authority to “enjoin or restrain the operation” of these provisions. Absent a clear textual authorization for this alternative vehicle—and given that accepting it would invite end-runs around the INA’s carefully reticulated scheme—I would dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: As a threshold matter, the suit seeks broad injunctive relief that would effectively supervise and reorder DHS’s front-line border screening and processing decisions—an area where the Executive traditionally exercises substantial enforcement and resource-allocation discretion and where Article III courts are not authorized to issue generalized commands to “process more” or “process differently.” Even assuming some of the alleged turnbacks or delays could be unlawful, Congress in 8 U.S.C. § 1252 largely channeled review of removal-related claims into the INA’s specialized review scheme, and the plaintiffs’ “access-to-asylum” theories functionally arise from and are intertwined with the inspection/expedited-removal machinery at the border, bringing them within § 1252’s channeling limits rather than freestanding APA district-court review. Jennings underscores that § 1252(b)(9) is a sweeping channeling provision for claims connected to removal and its predicates, and Thuraissigiam confirms that, at least for recent unlawful entrants subject to expedited removal, Congress may sharply restrict the forum and scope of judicial review without creating a broad, systemic cause of action in district court. Because the requested relief would circumvent the INA’s review architecture and would require ongoing judicial management of border operations, the complaint should be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction/reviewability under § 1252.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The threshold question is jurisdiction, and respondents’ claims—though styled as “access-to-asylum” challenges—seek judicial supervision of DHS’s implementation of § 1225/expedited-removal screening and related intake decisions at the border, which Congress broadly channeled into the INA’s exclusive review scheme in 8 U.S.C. § 1252 (including § 1252(b)(9)’s consolidation of claims “arising from” removal proceedings and § 1252(a)(2)’s limits on review of discretionary/processing judgments). Given IIRIRA’s design to protect the Executive’s administration of the removal system from systemic district-court litigation, the requested classwide, programmatic relief is the kind of interference Congress foreclosed absent express authorization. To the extent respondents invoke constitutional minima, Thuraissigiam confirms that Congress may sharply restrict judicial review for noncitizens at or near the border and that courts may not expand review beyond what the statute permits. Because respondents have not identified a statutory grant allowing this pre-removal, systemic suit in district court, it must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Starting with the INA’s text and structure, the jurisdiction-stripping provisions in 8 U.S.C. § 1252 generally channel review of removal-related determinations into the petition-for-review process tied to removal proceedings, but respondents’ claims (as framed) target systemic, pre-removal policies and practices that allegedly block people from accessing the statutory right to “apply for asylum” under § 1158 and the inspection/asylum-screening steps in § 1225—not the validity of any final order of removal. Section 1252(g), as construed in AADC, is a narrow bar limited to claims “arising from” the Executive’s decisions to commence, adjudicate, or execute removal proceedings; alleged turnbacks and port-of-entry access barriers precede (and often prevent) the initiation of any proceeding, making it difficult to classify these claims as within § 1252’s core channeling scheme. And even where § 1252’s limits arguably bear on the case, respondents’ challenge is best understood as raising at least a “question of law” about whether DHS has legal authority to adopt practices that categorically impede access to the asylum application process—an issue that, under the statute’s own design, is not the sort of discretionary, unreviewable judgment Congress “specified” to be in the agency’s discretion. Given that statutory fit, I would not dismiss for want of jurisdiction, while recognizing that § 1252(f)(1) may constrain the availability and breadth of injunctive relief.
